I’m looking for a dedicated team member with a strong background in physics and space concepts to collaborate, exchange knowledge, and build something impactful together.
summary:
Mountain valleys are hit hard by flash floods, and the damage is often invisible once the water recedes. Live coverage rarely reaches these areas, so residents receive aid late.
DNOV_1 built Atlas After Blue, a tool that uses NASA NISAR radar to show flood-related changes on the ground, even after the water is gone and through cloud cover. We demonstrate it on Kandia Gol, Pakistan, a valley that faced the same problem in the July 2026 floods. 
The method compares two radar images of the same area, taken from the same angle before and after the flood. Spots that clearly darkened and now look like calm water are marked as possible flood. Existing lakes and rivers are ignored, tiny scattered dots are removed as noise, and brighter areas are kept separate as uncertain change. The result is reported as possible flooding, not confirmed, because no ground check was possible at this site.
The result is presented through an interactive map and a before-and-after slider, so disaster-management teams can review changes and prioritize response and recovery. Everything is explained in simple terms on our website, with sources and a full report.
details:
Atlas After Blue: Final Project Brief

What it does

Atlas After Blue (AAB) is a web app that uses NISAR L-band radar to map candidate flood change after a flash flood. It compares two scenes of the same area, taken from the same track, frame, and direction (Track 84, Frame 19, ascending). We demonstrate it on the 22 July 2026 flash flood in Kandia Gol, Upper Kohistan, using scenes from 14 and 26 July.

Why floods

Pakistan has only one coastline, yet floods strike again and again. The worst damage is often in mountain valleys, where rescue teams arrive late. By the time live coverage reaches them, the destruction has already happened. A documented, traceable record of what changed helps authorities understand the damage and plan for the future.

How it works

The method is a transparent rule, not machine learning. We bypassed machine learning because there is no ground truth to train or test it.

  • Calm water reflects radar away, so it looks dark.
  • A pixel is a candidate flood if it got at least 3 dB darker and is now at or below -14 dB.
  • Permanent water is excluded, and groups smaller than 4 pixels (400 m²) are removed as speckle.
  • Areas that got at least 3.5 dB brighter are kept separate as uncertain change.

Result: 55 candidate patches covering 0.0278 km², with 11.56 km² of uncertain surface change. Confidence is low and unvalidated. We say "candidate flood," never confirmed floodwater.

Five pages: Home (before/after and key figures), Report (interactive map, swipe, side-by-side, history strip, limitations), Method (interactive explainers, pixel tester, glossary), Sources (every file, scene ID and link), About (name, audience, team, AI declaration).

Impact

AAB supports provincial disaster-management teams such as PDMA in reviewing satellite observations alongside situation reports. It helps ground teams decide where to check first. It is supplementary evidence and does not replace field assessment. It also shows that NASA's open data can serve a small team in Pakistan. When we shared the site with friends, they were surprised: they thought NASA only works on space and Mars But now their thinking has changed, and they value how NASA resources can be useful for the local community.

Creativity

  • One name, two stories: "Atlas After Blue" maps the land after the water has gone, and "AAB" is aab (آب), the Urdu word for water.
  • NASA data for ordinary people: we wanted to bring this science to everyday people, not only big companies.
  • Understandable by anyone: interactive explainers and a plain-English glossary mean even a 5th-grade student can follow how the satellite works.
  • Radar made less scary: a clear before/after comparison sits at the top of the Home page, which also sparks curiosity about science.
  • Nothing to take on trust: the Sources page lets anyone check every file, scene ID and link.
  • Honesty as a feature: four days after the peak, radar saw little standing water. We show that plainly.

Factors we considered

Four-day gap after the peak (no satellite coverage 19 to 24 July), debris-laden flash floods looking bright instead of dark, radar shadow hiding about 14% of the area, channels narrower than about 20 m being lost at 10 m resolution, provisional data with no field validation, and mixed viewing angles creating false change.

Tools

  • Data: NISAR L2 GCOV (HH, 10 m) via ASF Search API and ASF Vertex; PDMA KP situation reports.
  • Processing: 16-stage Python pipeline.
  • Front end: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet 1.9.4; GeoJSON and JSON.
  • Software and services: VS Code, ClickUp, GitHub, Netlify, Porkbun.
  • Hardware: personal laptops and a Wi-Fi network.

AI declaration

AI was an assistant, not a decision-maker. The logo idea and colors were ours, and ChatGPT turned them into an image. Gemini and Claude helped write repetitive code to save time, but the team analyzed it and ran the pipeline. What goes where, the buttons, the thresholds and the wording were all team decisions. On the site, each tool has a short label to avoid clutter, with a note below explaining AI's assisting role.
